nameStory: The scientific name 'calcar' comes from Latin meaning 'spur,' likely referring to some small projection or spine on this harvestman's body. Like other harvestmen, this species gets its common group name from the old belief that they could predict good weather for harvesting crops by their leg movements.
description: Leiobunum calcar is a harvestman, often called a 'daddy longlegs,' though it's not actually a spider. Like other harvestmen, it has an oval body that appears to be all one piece, unlike spiders which have a distinct waist between their front and back sections. These arachnids have extremely long, thin legs that can span several inches, making them appear much larger than their small pea-sized bodies. They're gentle creatures that pose no threat to humans.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Single oval body segment without the pinched waist that spiders have - looks like a small brown or gray bean with legs attached

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Eight incredibly long, thin legs that feel delicate and thread-like if gently touched - they can detach easily as a defense mechanism

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body is typically pea-sized or smaller, but leg span can reach 2-3 inches across

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with a characteristic bouncing, swaying motion and often forms loose congregations with other harvestmen

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Two small eyes positioned on a tiny raised bump on top of the body, unlike spiders which typically have eight eyes

habitat: Found in wooded areas, gardens, and areas with leaf litter throughout New England. They prefer moist environments and are often discovered under logs, in tall grass, or climbing on vegetation during evening hours. Look for them in shaded areas where the ground stays damp and organic matter accumulates.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often found congregating under logs or debris where they overwintered.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible, often seen climbing on plants or gathering in groups on tree trunks and walls in the evening.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek sheltered overwintering sites under logs, leaf litter, or other protected locations.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically hibernate in protected spots like under bark or in deep leaf litter, becoming inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: When threatened, harvestmen can intentionally detach their legs, which continue to twitch and move for several minutes afterward - this creates a distraction while the harvestman escapes, though unlike some lizards, the legs never grow back.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with cellar spiders (also called 'daddy longlegs'), but harvestmen have a single body segment while cellar spiders have the typical spider waist. Remember: harvestmen have 'one piece bodies' while spiders are 'two piece puzzles.'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'daddy longlegs' causes confusion because it's used for harvestmen, cellar spiders, and even crane flies in different regions. True harvestmen like this species are in the order Opiliones, not Araneae like true spiders, making them more like arachnid cousins than spider siblings.
compareHints: Distinguishing Leiobunum calcar from other harvestmen in its genus requires close examination of subtle features like leg length ratios and body markings. The Eastern Harvestman (L. vittatum) is more commonly encountered and tends to be slightly larger. Without magnification, most Leiobunum species appear very similar and are best identified as part of the broader harvestman group.
